title: Alexander & the Hellenistic Turn
subtitle: From Achaemenid rule to the Macedonian conquest of the Levant and Egypt.

chapters.title: Pella and Macedon
chapters.description: Begin at Pella, the royal center from which Alexander’s Asian campaign emerged.

chapters.title: Tyre and Gaza
chapters.description: Alexander’s conquest of Tyre and Gaza is securely historical. The app does not add the much later Josephus story of Alexander in Jerusalem as an established event.

chapters.title: Egypt and Alexandria
chapters.description: The campaign enters Egypt and Alexandria is founded, setting up the Ptolemaic world in which a major Jewish diaspora develops.

title: Ptolemaic Judea & Alexandria
subtitle: Third-century BCE Judea between Jerusalem, Egyptian rule, documentary papyri, and the Greek-speaking diaspora.

chapters.title: Alexandria
chapters.description: Alexandria becomes a major Hellenistic metropolis and Jewish intellectual center.

chapters.title: Greek Torah
chapters.description: The Greek Torah emerges in Ptolemaic Egypt. The familiar seventy-two-translator story is not treated as stenographic history.

chapters.title: Jerusalem under Ptolemaic hegemony
chapters.description: The timeline shows a Ptolemaic sphere around Judea, but not a year-exact provincial border.

title: From Ptolemy to Seleucus
subtitle: Panium, Antiochus III, temple administration, and the changing imperial framework before the revolt.

chapters.title: Panium
chapters.description: Antiochus III’s victory near Panium shifts Coele-Syria and Judea into Seleucid control.

chapters.title: Antioch
chapters.description: Antioch is the political center of the dynasty now ruling Judea.

chapters.title: Temple administration
chapters.description: Seleucid administrative inscriptions illuminate temple oversight but do not independently verify the miraculous scene in 2 Maccabees 3.

title: Antiochus IV & the Jerusalem Crisis
subtitle: High-priestly conflict, Seleucid intervention, the Acra, and the crisis that precipitated revolt.

chapters.title: Antiochus IV
chapters.description: Antiochus IV comes to the throne in a dynasty already under Roman and fiscal pressures.

chapters.title: Jerusalem divided
chapters.eyebrow: 169–167 BCE · literary sources differ in emphasis
chapters.description: Onias III, Jason and Menelaus belong to a high-priestly and civic crisis remembered differently by 1 and 2 Maccabees.

chapters.title: The Acra problem
chapters.description: The Acra is central to the Maccabean narratives, but the app refuses to draw a definitive fortress footprint until competing archaeological proposals are explicitly modeled.

title: The Maccabean Revolt
subtitle: Modein, Emmaus, temple rededication, Beth-zechariah, Adasa, and Elasa.

chapters.title: Modein
chapters.description: The revolt begins at Modein in 1 Maccabees. The town remains unpinned because its exact archaeological identification is debated.

chapters.title: Emmaus
chapters.description: Judas defeats a Seleucid force near Emmaus; the site is a strong Maccabean-period identification.

chapters.title: Jerusalem rededicated
chapters.description: The temple is rededicated, later commemorated as Hanukkah. No excavated surface is labeled as the exact altar of 164 BCE.

chapters.title: Beth-zechariah
chapters.description: A major Seleucid counterattack includes war elephants in 1 Maccabees; the battlefield anchor remains a candidate.

chapters.title: Judas dies
chapters.description: The final battle at Elasa is historically narrated but geographically unresolved, so the story zooms to the broader region rather than inventing a pin.

title: From Revolt to Hasmonean State
subtitle: Jonathan, Simon, John Hyrcanus, territorial expansion, kingship, and the dynasty’s internal tensions.

chapters.title: Jonathan and high priesthood
chapters.description: Jonathan’s rise shows the revolt becoming institutional power within a still-Seleucid diplomatic world.

chapters.title: Simon and independence
chapters.eyebrow: 142–141 BCE · transition, not a single instant
chapters.description: Tribute remission and evacuation of the Acra mark stages in the emergence of effective independence.

chapters.title: Idumea incorporated
chapters.description: Maresha and Adora anchor the southern expansion. Josephus’s account of compelled customs is presented as later literary testimony, not a modern ethnicity polygon.

chapters.title: Gerizim sanctuary destroyed
chapters.description: A major Hellenistic sanctuary is archaeologically real; assigning its destruction precisely to John Hyrcanus is a strong but interpretive correlation.

chapters.title: Kingship and expansion
chapters.description: Aristobulus I and Alexander Jannaeus turn priestly rule into monarchy; the political map changes repeatedly rather than displaying one permanent Hasmonean border.

title: Second Temple Judaism Beyond One Map
subtitle: Jerusalem, Gerizim, Alexandria, Leontopolis, Qumran, manuscripts, and competing communities.

chapters.title: Jerusalem temple
chapters.description: Jerusalem remains the major Judean cultic center, yet Second Temple Jewish and Samaritan life is geographically diverse.

chapters.title: Mount Gerizim
chapters.description: Gerizim provides a securely excavated alternative sacred center with its own inscriptions and community history.

chapters.title: Alexandria
chapters.description: Greek-speaking Jewish life flourishes in Ptolemaic and later Roman Alexandria.

chapters.title: Leontopolis
chapters.eyebrow: Onias temple tradition · site precision limited
chapters.description: Josephus describes another Jewish temple in Egypt; the atlas treats Tell el-Yahudiya as a candidate region rather than a recovered sanctuary footprint.

chapters.title: Qumran and the scrolls
chapters.eyebrow: Late Second Temple · archaeology without forced sect label
chapters.description: The site and manuscripts are real; whether “Qumran = Essenes” explains every feature remains an interpretive model rather than a map certainty.

title: Nabataea, Idumea & the Southern Corridors
subtitle: Petra, Maresha, caravan trade, Idumean incorporation, and the background to the Herodian family.

chapters.title: Petra
chapters.eyebrow: Nabataean kingdom · monumental growth through time
chapters.description: Petra anchors Nabataean power, but the map does not project later monumental facades unchanged into the second century BCE.

chapters.title: Across the Negev
chapters.description: Avdat belongs to a wider network connecting Arabia, the Negev and Mediterranean ports such as Gaza.

chapters.title: Idumea
chapters.description: Maresha’s archaeology shows a diverse Hellenistic city before Hasmonean incorporation; later Herodian ancestry emerges from this Idumean context.

title: Rome Enters Judea
subtitle: Hasmonean civil war, Pompey, Roman Syria, and the end of independent Hasmonean kingship.

chapters.title: Dynastic conflict
chapters.eyebrow: 67–63 BCE · Hyrcanus II vs Aristobulus II
chapters.description: A Hasmonean succession dispute draws in neighboring and then Roman power.

chapters.title: Pompey in Syria
chapters.description: Pompey’s Syrian command provides the regional base for intervention.

chapters.title: Jerusalem captured
chapters.description: Pompey captures Jerusalem. The event is secure; exact siege lines remain a later-source reconstruction.

chapters.title: A Roman political world
chapters.description: Hyrcanus II remains high priest while Antipater grows in influence inside a Roman-dominated eastern Mediterranean.

title: Herod & the Roman Transition
subtitle: Rome, Jerusalem, Actium, Rhodes, and the architecture that forms the immediate background to the Gospels.

chapters.title: Named king in Rome
chapters.description: The Senate recognizes Herod as king, but he does not yet control Jerusalem.

chapters.title: Jerusalem, 37 BCE
chapters.description: Herod captures Jerusalem and removes Antigonus II, beginning effective rule.

chapters.title: Actium
chapters.description: Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra; Herod must renegotiate his position with the victor.

chapters.title: Rhodes
chapters.description: Josephus describes Herod meeting Octavian on Rhodes; the maritime path is schematic.

chapters.title: Jerusalem rebuilt
chapters.description: Herod’s expansion transforms the Temple Mount. The platform is archaeological fact; sanctuary reconstructions remain models.

chapters.title: Caesarea Maritima
chapters.description: Caesarea embodies Herod’s Roman-facing monumental program and becomes essential for the Acts-era map to come.
